utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Case number IT-04-80-I, the Prosecutor versus Zdravko Tolimir, Radivoje Miletic, and Milan Gvero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Good afternoon to you. Mr. Miletic, before we proceed any further, I would like to make sure that you are receiving interpretation in a language that you can understand, that you understand. I will repeat. Before we proceed any further, I want to make sure that you are receiving interpretation in a language which you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not receiving any interpretation into the Serbian language. All I can hear is the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you check the channel on -- on his receiver, please. It should be on channel 6, I think. I will -- I will repeat. Mr. Miletic, before we proceed any further, I want to make sure that you are receiving interpretation in a language which you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am receiving interpretation in a language that I understand now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. If at any time during the proceedings there are problems with interpretation -- in other words, if at any time you are not receiving interpretation in your language -- please draw my attention straight away.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The answer was not audible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, could you repeat your answer, please, because I could not -- the interpreters did not hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Mr. Gvero, the same procedure with you. I want to make sure before we proceed any further that you are receiving interpretation in a language which you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. And the same advice: If at any time there are problems with interpretation, please draw my attention immediately.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Peter McCloskey for the Prosecution, assisted by Janet Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Mr. Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Peter Morrissey, and I appear as duty counsel only today on behalf of Mr. Miletic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, and I note that you are appearing as duty counsel. Appearance for Mr. Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Steven Powles, similarly appearing as duty counsel for Mr. Milan Gvero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Powles, as well and good afternoon to you both. Now, I will give a start now to the procedure proper relating to the Initial Appearance. And before I do so, I wish to advise you, Mr. Miletic and Mr. Gvero, that in terms of both the Statute and the Rules of Evidence and Procedure of this Tribunal, you have a right to remain silent. I suppose you know already what that means. Basically it means that no one can force you to answer any questions or to say anything in this Tribunal from now onwards. You are here because an indictment has been issued and confirmed against you by this Tribunal, and I will start by first of all giving some details about this indictment. I understand that you will later on be waiving your right to have it read out in full, but I think it's fit and proper that I do give some details arising out of this indictment not only for your own sake but also for the public that will be following these proceedings. Mr. Miletic and Mr. Gvero, you are included in the indictment which carries the number IT-04-80-I. This indictment was confirmed by my colleague Judge Daqun Liu on the 10th of February of this year and actually relates to three persons, the two of you and Zdravko Tolimir, who is not here today. The case -- or the existence of the indictment was made public as regards you, Mr. Miletic, and you, Mr. Gvero, following the decision of the Judge -- of Judge Liu of the 23rd of February of this year, and subsequently the indictment was also made public in regard -- in relation to the other co-accused, Zdravko Tolimir, as a result of the -- another decision taken again by Judge Liu two days later; namely, on the 25th of February of this year. I take it that you, Mr. Miletic - correct me if I'm wrong - you surrendered to the custody of this Tribunal and that you arrived at the seat of this Tribunal here in The Hague this week; namely, two days ago, on -- precisely on the 28th of February, 2005. While you, Mr. Gvero, I'm informed you surrendered to the custody of this Tribunal and arrived last week, on the 24th of February, 2005. I decided to combine the -- your Initial Appearance with that of Mr. Miletic because I was informed that Mr. Miletic's arrival was imminent and therefore there was no point in having two separate Initial Appearances. Otherwise, I would have held the Initial Appearance before. The indictment against you states that during the time period relevant to the events which are described in it, Zdravko Tolimir was the assistant commander for intelligence and security of the Main Staff of the Bosnian Serb army. Henceforth I will refer to this army as the "VRS" for short. At the time, you, Mr. Miletic, was, according to the Prosecution, chief of operations and training -- of operations and training and Deputy Chief of Staff or was standing in for the Chief of Staff, and also of the main staff of the VRS, while according to the indictment you, Mr. Gvero, was assistant commander for morale, legal, and religious affairs of the Main Staff of the VRS. According to the indictment, the three of you- that's Mr. Tolimir, you, Mr. Miletic, and you, Mr. Gvero, are individually criminally responsible for the acts or omissions of your -- of your subordinates pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute of this Tribunal. Basically this means that the three of you are charged with having committed, planned, instigated, ordered, or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation, and execution of the crimes which are brought -- of which you -- with which you are charged and which I will mention very shortly. The three accused are charged with the following counts as set forth in the said indictment: You have against you, Mr. Miletic and Mr. Gvero, four counts of crimes against humanity, which are grounded under Article 5 of the Statute of this Tribunal, these being murder, persecutions on political, racial, and religious grounds, inhumane acts, that is, forcible transfer, and deportation, and in addition one count of violations of the laws or customs of war, which is grounded under Article 3 of the Statute of the Tribunal, consisting in a charge of murder. The indictment alleges that the three of you - that is, Mr. Tolimir, you, Mr. Miletic, and you, Mr. Gvero - together with other VRS and MUP, Ministry of Internal Affairs officers and units and Republika Srpska officials which are -- or who are identified in the indictment, the Prosecution alleges that you were members of and knowingly participated in a joint criminal enterprise and operation, the common purpose of which was to force the Muslim population out of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves to areas outside the control of the -- of Republika Srpska from 11th March 1995 through the end of August 1995. According to the Prosecution, the execution of the joint criminal enterprise and operation to force the Muslim population out of the areas of Srebrenica and Zepa actually began in 1992, when the VRS and Republika Srpska forces began attacking towns and villages in Eastern Bosnia, such as Bijeljina and Zvornik, and forcing the Muslim population to move southwards, towards the area of Srebrenica and Zepa. According to the Prosecution, the joint criminal enterprise and operation to force the Muslims from the areas of Srebrenica and Zepa continued despite the formation by the United Nations of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves on the 6th of May, 1993 as a result of Security Council Resolution number 824. The Prosecutor alleges that throughout 1993, 1994, and 1995 the authorities of the Republika Srpska continued to press for the departure of the Muslims from Srebrenica and Zepa. The charges that are the subject of the indictment that I mentioned earlier focus on the alleged joint criminal enterprise and operation which continued from 11th March 1995, when the policy to remove the Muslim population from Srebrenica and Zepa, according to the Prosecutor, was formally enunciated by the then-President Radovan Karadzic in directive number 7 and through the end of August 1995, when all the Muslims from Srebrenica and Zepa had been forced from the homes in the enclaves to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The indictment further states: "In order to achieve the goal of the joint criminal enterprise and operation as expressed in Presidential Directive number 7, to force the Muslim populations out of Srebrenica and Zepa, namely, to leave the area, several actions were carried out, included but not limited to the following" -- this is what the Prosecutor alleges. "(a), making life unbearable for the inhabitants of the enclave; Two, defeating the Muslim forces militarily; Three, disabling the local United Nations forces militarily; Four, preventing and controlling outside international protection of the enclaves, including airstrikes and international monitoring; and Finally, controlling the movement of people out of the enclaves." According to the indictment, members of the joint criminal enterprise and operation made life unbearable for the inhabitants of the enclave by means of shelling civilian targets in Srebrenica Zepa, and secondly, restricting humanitarian aid, such as convoys of food, medicine, and medical assistance despite, notwithstanding, dire shortages in the enclaves. The indictment further alleges that: "It was foreseeable to Zdravko Tolimir, Radivoje Miletic, and Milan Gvero that individual criminal acts such as individual killings described in this indictment in paragraphs 52 and 53 and acts of persecution, described in paragraphs 54(b) and (c) of this indictment, would be carried out by the Serb forces during the joint criminal enterprise and operation to forcibly transfer and deport the populations of Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves." The indictment does list the members -- the other members of the joint criminal enterprise, and I'm going to read out the names. From Republika Srpska, President Radovan Karadzic, General Ratko Mladic, the commander of the VRS, General Milenko Zivanovic, commander of the Drina Corps through about 20 hours on 13th July, 1995; general Radislav Krstic, Chief of Staff deputy commander through about 20 hours on the 13th of July, 1995 and thereafter commander of the Drina Corps; Colonel Petar Salapura, Chief of Intelligence of the Main Staff; Colonel Ljubisa Beara, chief of security of the Main Staff; Colonel Radislav Jankovic, intelligence officer of the Main Staff; Major Dragomir Pecanac, security officer of the Main Staff; Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic, commander of the Bratunac Brigade; Captain Momir Nikolic, chief of security and intelligence, Bratunac Brigade; Colonel Vinko Pandurevic, commander of the Zvornik Brigade; Lieutenant Colonel Dragan Obrenovic, deputy commander and Chief of Staff of the Zvornik Brigade; Lieutenant Colonel Rajko Krsmanovic, Drina Corps chief of transportation services; Colonel Lazar Acamovic, Drina Corps assistant commander for rear services; Ljubisa Borovcanin, commander of Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior special police brigade. Various others, individuals, military police units were involved, according to the Prosecutor, in the operation to forcibly transfer and deport the Muslim population of Srebrenica and Zepa. This is in essence what is contained in the indictment against you. I wish to inform you that by the order of the President of this Tribunal, Theodor Meron, dated 24th February 2005, and the order of the Vice-President of this Tribunal, Fausto Pocar, dated the 28th of February, 2005, this case was assigned to my Trial Chamber, that is, Trial Chamber II. Subsequently by an order dated 1st of March, 2005 - that's yesterday - I designated myself as the Pre-Trial Judge for the purpose of today's Initial Appearance for -- for the Initial Appearance of both of you. Having premised all this, I will now proceed to conduct the procedural part of the Initial Appearance. In terms of -- I'll do this in terms of Rule 62 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, following which I will then be turning my attention to you, again Mr. Miletic and Mr. Gvero, and ask you whether you are prepared to enter a plea to the charges that have been brought against you by the Prosecutor. Mr. Miletic, could you stand up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: According to Rule 62 but also according to the Statute, I am tasked with the responsibility of making sure of a few details. I asked in the beginning of the sitting for your legal representation, and I was informed by Mr. Morrissey that he as duty counsel -- has been appointed duty counsel. Basically that means that he has been appointed for the purpose of this Initial Appearance and nothing else. I first of all want to know whether you are aware of this, that Mr. Morrissey is appointed only for the purpose of today's Initial Appearance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And do you have any remarks or any comments on -- on this or matters related to your representation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objections to Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it that you will be then dealing directly with the registrar as regards the appointment of the counsel that will follow, that will look after your interests for the purposes of the pre-trial proceedings and subsequently for the trial itself?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since you have given me the opportunity, when I said that I surrendered to this Tribunal -- when you said that I surrendered to this Tribunal, I didn't surrender. A general doesn't surrender. I came voluntarily. I didn't surrender to anyone. That's the first thing I would like to point out. Secondly, I asked for a lawyer, and I would like that lawyer to be lead counsel or co-counsel in my case, since from the time that my lawyer established contact with the Registry, which was on the 2nd or 3rd of December, I was then first asked to give a statement as a suspect and as of that date there was communication between my lawyer and the OTP, the Prosecution, and I'm surprised to hear that there is a problem with regard to Defence counsel of my choice. I would like to ask you to grant me the right I have to choose my own lawyer in the interest of justice, in the interest of my case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The -- Mr. Miletic, the right of the accused to counsel of his own choice is not absolute; it is limited. And in the case of this Tribunal, it is limited by what is provided by our Rules and directives. The person who is entrusted by the instruments of this Tribunal to deal directly with this matter is first and foremost the registrar, and the registrar knows exactly what his obligations are. I am not aware, simply because this is only the Initial Appearance until now -- I am not aware of the problems that you have mentioned because obviously there has not been any correspondence or any contacts between myself or my Chamber and the registrar. But if there are problems in which the Trial Chamber can intervene, then I take it that you have and you should granted all the opportunity to bring those problems to my attention. What I can promise you is that I will give them all due consideration but nothing beyond that for the time being because, as I said, much that relates to the assignment of counsel falls within the prerogative and the discretion of the registrar. We intervene only when that discretion is not exercised in a reasonable manner. But I would be, of course, very much interested in knowing what the problem is, if indeed it exists, and only if it is not solved between -- between you and -- and the registrar. I am -- I don't know if Mr. Morrissey is aware of this and whether he can be of any assistance. I don't think I can be of any further assistance, Mr. Morrissey. I'm sure you understand my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage it may be that the matter can be resolved. There are some hopeful signs that it can be. I -- I can say that the Registry are having ongoing discussions and that -- that Mr. Miletic has been consistent in -- in the position that he's put to this Court, which he's entitled to do and entitled to press for counsel of his own choice. The Registry is aware of matters. It doesn't appear to me - and I can indicate to the Court now - that it doesn't appear to me that an impasse has been reached. I think that ongoing discussions are occurring. And since there still is hope that a resolution will happen, we shouldn't invoke the Tribunal's direct involvement at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. I appreciate that, Mr. Morrissey. Mr. Miletic, you've heard what your duty counsel has just stated, so I would suggest that we leave the matter here, where it stands, and then we'll take it up later on, if at all necessary. Because in the meantime an agreement may -- may be reached between you and the registrar. But if there is no such agreement, please do bring that to my attention, and I'll see to what extent the Trial Chamber can intervene. You may sit down. Thank you. [The accused sits down].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gvero, could you stand up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Gvero, it's more or less the same procedure. You know that for the purpose of today's appearance, Initial Appearance, Mr. Powles has been appointed. I do not imagine that you have any objections to that, and assuming that you don't, I would like to know if you have any remarks that you would like to make here and now on matters related to your representation for the purpose of the pre-trial and also the trial proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for giving me this opportunity to say something. The problem with counsel is something I see as a big handicap at the outset. While I was still in Belgrade, I chose a lawyer I know, attorney Tomislav Visnjic. I was convinced that he would be fully able to appear for me before this Tribunal. I still believe that there is a possibility for him to be appointed my Defence counsel. Secondly, last night I wrote and this morning I submitted the name of another lawyer who, as far I know, meets all the requirements to represent me before this Tribunal. This is Mr. Dragan Krgovic, an attorney from Belgrade. Should there be any problems with either one of these two attorneys, I would like this to be solved as soon as possible because time is passing and this is to my detriment. I also wish to say the following: In agreement with the government of Serbia, I arrived voluntarily to appear before this Tribunal firmly convinced that there is a large potential here for justice and truth to come to light, and I believe that all those participating in these proceedings wish the same. As I am a calm person by nature and I feel that there are some misunderstandings in connection with these charges, I am sure that the truth will soon come to light to everyone's satisfaction. I only wish to ask that the supporting material with the indictment be delivered to me as soon as possible, since I have no counsel, because I am not able to organise any gathering of material. Mr. President, my problem will be in that the job I had in the army and the Main Staff was a very special one and this will be difficult to demonstrate in any great detail; however, I will do my best to assist this Tribunal to arrive at the truth. And finally, by your leave, I assure you, as a moral and responsible person, that I did not kill so much as a sparrow throughout the war, let alone a person, and I did not have any units under my command. My job was information, morale, and cooperation with other institutions. I performed my job deeply convinced that I was doing it properly. I was not fighting against any nation but against the ideology leading nations into war against each other, and I hope to be able to prove this. That's all I wanted to say for now. Thank you, and please assist me to resolve the problem of my counsel as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Gvero. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, my advice to you is that first you proceed with the discussions with the registrar, who is the person, as I explained earlier, entrusted with -- with the task of assigning counsel and co-counsel and legal assistants to each one of you, also in deciding matters relating to legal aid if there is an application for legal aid. For the time being, I am not aware of any problems. I take it that you will, like Mr. Miletic, inform the Trial Chamber if there are problems with the assignment of -- assigning of -- of counsel of your choice, and my task then as Pre-Trial Judge or as President of Trial Chamber II will be to see if it's the case of intervening or -- or not. But for the time being, all I can do is to ask you to proceed with the discussions that you have already undertaken with the registrar of this Tribunal. And with regard to the rest, I can assure you that whatever you have stated has gone on the records of this case and will remain there. Mr. Powles, I don't know if you can be of any assistance in relation to the matters raised by your client as regards representation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if you are aware of the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Perhaps no more than Your Honour. To a limited extent, Your Honour, yes. May I firstly echo and endorse the comments made by my learned friend Mr. Morrissey on behalf of his client. A similar position pertains to Mr. Gvero. Secondly, may I for the record state that obviously as duty counsel only appearing on behalf of Mr. Gvero here today on a temporary basis, and he has been informed of that. Thirdly, and also for the record, may I respectfully request that the registrar deals with the issue of representation for Mr. Gvero as a matter of priority and deal with it as soon as possible. Obviously certain matters that need to be dealt with imminently; for example, an application on provisional release, could only be undertaken and carried out once permanent counsel is assigned. So on behalf of Mr. Gvero, may I again respectfully ask that the matter is given the utmost and urgent attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, Mr. Powles. I don't think it's the case for me to enter any order to the registrar to that effect because, from my experience here, the registrar does take these matters -- does give to these matters his utmost and immediate attention, and it's only when there are real problems that a delay in the decision-taking process occurs. However, I will, of course, Mr. Powles, when this Initial Appearance is over, try to find out with the registrar what these problems are, because I'm not aware of them. And as you can imagine, I don't come to the Initial Appearance and speak to the registrar before. I mean, it's simply not done. But I will check with him to -- to see what the problems are and what are the prospects of -- of a solution. I understand from what you have said that even in your case there doesn't seem to be a real impasse.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if there's no impasse, there's no point in me recommending to the registrar to do what he has always done.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I will leave it at that and I will take it up as President of Trial Chamber II with the registrar and see what the situation is. However, if this is prolonged, of course, I -- I take it that I -- it will be brought to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for that indication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: May I also indicate, of course, it doesn't appear that an impasse has been reached yet and one would hope that this matter can be resolved relatively smoothly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope so, Mr. Powles, and let's hope so. Yes. Now, Mr. Miletic, could you stand up, please, again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very soon I will be asking you whether you want to enter a plea to the charges that have been brought against you. But according to the Rules, before I do so, I am tasked with asking you a few questions. My first question to you: Could you kindly give me your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Radivoje Miletic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Radivoje, do you spell it with a final "E," Radivoje?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, with an "E" at the end, Radivoje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The second question: Just in case -- I know that in your country many individuals are also referred to by nicknames, like in my country. Do you have any nickname that others refer -- refer to you with?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were several of them. It depended on the situation. But I don't think it's relevant now. There were various nicknames that were used. I don't know whether it's necessary to list all of them. I don't think it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a question that I am asking. If you decide not to answer that question, you have every right not to answer it. But I am asking you the question, if you are -- and I -- if you are aware of any nicknames that apply to you, please let -- let us have them. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. There are documents in this record and nicknames will be an issue, and this could be a matter that -- which could be incriminating against the -- against the general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But I have warned him already of his right to remain silent. So if I were to recommend anything to you - although, strictly speaking I shouldn't be recommending - but taking advantage of what has just been said by the officer in charge of the Prosecution in this case, I would not insist on asking you to answer this question unless you prefer to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I have the opportunity to approach Mr. Miletic and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't see in court a -- an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can provide you with one. How can we solve this? We need someone who speaks the language.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: An interpreter from the booth could assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, an interpreter from the booth. But the interpreter would need to come into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, in those circumstances, might I approach, please. I don't think it's necessary to adjourn the court. I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think so. I mean, this is a very simple procedure anyway. Perhaps, Mr. Morrissey, you could ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. I'm grateful for the opportunity. I'm instructed that Mr. Miletic would prefer not to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to the Prosecutor for indicating that. Duty counsel are in a position of simply not knowing the significance of some of these questions, and so I put that on the record as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and I associate myself -- associate myself with the words of appreciation that you expressed in regard to the Prosecution. I thank you. My next question to you, Mr. Miletic, is your -- when were you born? Your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 6th of December, 1947.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And your place of birth. Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born in the village of Stovice [phoen] in Foca municipality in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a Serb, a citizen of the Federative Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I am going to ask you another question now. If you prefer -- the question is actually to give me the last address in which you resided before you came over here. Now, I understand that you may wish to answer or give this information in private session, because I don't think it is in anybody's interests, including your own, to have your -- your private address transmitted worldwide. So if you prefer to go in private session, we'll go into private session. Yes, Mr. Morrissey, I -- I take it you -- you can handle this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Instead of your client. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. And another thing. I take it you had a family, and I want to make sure that your family have -- are fully aware that you are here in The Hague and that you are being kept in custody at the Detention -- our Detention Unit in Scheveningen. Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are there any members of your family that you would like me to inform about your transfer here to The Hague and your state of detention here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. They have all been informed of the fact, all those who need to be aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The same question I put to you in relation to your embassy. I would imagine that your embassy is also aware of your transfer here to The Hague and your presence here. But if you think they are not or you would like me, as the Presiding Judge, to do anything on your behalf with the embassy of your country, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. They have been informed of the fact too. They were at the airport where they received me, so everything is fine as far as that is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gvero, we are going to go through the same procedure with you. We'll start with your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milan Gvero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Again, I ask you whether you have any nicknames by which you are known or referred to. If you think that by answering this question you might prejudice your position, please just tell me that you would like not to answer the question. Yes, Mr. Powles.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: I wonder if we could just pre-empt that by moving on and him not answering the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move to the next question. Your date of birth, please, Mr. Gvero?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no. No. No, I did not have any nicknames.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At least, not that I know of. My date of birth is the 4th of December, 1937.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And your place of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrkonjic Grad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For 30 years, I was a Yugoslav. After the break-up of Yugoslavia, I have been a citizen of Serbia and Montenegro, Serbia and Serbian Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Registrar. Again, the same two questions to you: Are the members of your family aware of your transfer here to The Hague and your state of detention in Scheveningen Detention Unit, or would you like me to inform some member of your family about this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I informed them personally. They saw me off. They all know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the same question in relation to your embassy, the Embassy of Serbia and Montenegro. I take it that they are aware of your presence here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the airport I was met by a lady from the embassy, but I wish to ask you to inform the embassy that I am having problems with the assignment of counsel, Defence counsel, and that they should assist me as far as they are able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. In this regard, registrar, please could you block copy, this part of the transcript; in other words, from page 24, line 5 to where I will finish making this statement, and the statement that I am making is that this part will be communicated by the registrar of this Tribunal -- it will be copied. It will be extracted from the transcript and copied and communicated by means of -- and not verbal or in any other manner that the registrar deems fit -- to the Secretariat of the Embassy of Serbia and Montenegro here in The Hague for their information. Thank you. So you've heard me say that this part of your statement together with mine will be communicated to the secretary of your embassy and then it's up to them to do anything, if it's the case of doing anything. All right. Now, you may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You may sit down. [The accused sits down].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, as accused before this Tribunal, you enjoy a certain number of rights. These rights are incorporated in the Statute of this Tribunal but also relatively in the Rules which are a reflection of what is contained in the Statute. I am going to ask the registrar to read out aloud to you Articles 20 and 21 of the Statute of this Tribunal, which list the rights to which you are entitled. And when I say "you are entitled," it means that you are entitled to them from now until the end of the proceedings. Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Article 20 of the Statute reads as follows: "Commencement and conduct of trial proceedings. Point 1: The Trial Chambers shall ensure that a trial is fair an expeditious, and that proceedings are conducted in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence with full respect for the rights of the accused and due regard for the protection of victims and witnesses. "2, a person against whom an indictment has been confirmed shall, pursuant to an order or an arrest warrant of the International Tribunal be taken into custody, immediately informed of the charges against him, and transferred to the International Tribunal. "3, the Trial Chamber shall read the indictment, satisfy itself that the rights of the accused are respected, confirm that the accused understands the indictment, and instruct the accused to enter a plea. The Trial Chamber shall then set the date for trial. "4, the hearings shall be public unless the Trial Chamber decides to close the proceedings in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence." Article 21 of the Statute reads as follows: "Rights of the accused. "1, all persons shall be equal before the International Tribunal. "2, in the determination of charges against him, the accused shall be entitled to a fair and public hearing subject to Article 22 of the Statute. "3, the accused shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to the provisions of the present Statute. "4, in the determination of any charge against the accused pursuant to the present Statute, the accused shall be entitled to the following minimum guarantees in full equality: (a), to be informed promptly and in detail in a language which he understands of the nature and cause of the charge against him; (b), to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence and to communicate with counsel of his own choosing; (c), to be tried without undue delay; (d), to be tried in his presence and to defend himself in person or through legal assistance of his own choosing, to be informed if he does not have legal assistance of this right and to have legal assistance assigned to him in any case where the interests of justice so require and without payment by him in any such case if he does not have sufficient means to pay for it; (e), to examine or have examined the witness against -- the witnesses against him and to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses on his behalf and under the same conditions as a witness against him; (f), to have the free assistance of an interpreter if he cannot understand or speak the language used in the International Tribunal; (g), not to be compelled to testify against him or to confess guilt." Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you -- I thank you, Mr. Registrar. Now, having gone through these two Articles, it is obvious that I have to make sure of certain basic matters. Mr. Miletic, could you stand up again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've heard the registrar read out these two articles, which basically embody the minimum safeguards, the minimum rights for -- for a fair trial, the minimum rights that you enjoy too. Do you understand the importance of these rights?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure that you have received a formal copy of the indictment in your own language. Could you confirm that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have received such a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I take it that you have read it. And if you have, then I would like to know from you whether you have understood the import of its contents. Basically whether you are aware what it -- it alleges against you and what it charges you with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have read the indictment on a number of occasions, but I have not understood it, and I am surprised by the legal and factual description of the events contained in the indictment, and this is an issue that I will have to clarify when I have the opportunity of conferring with my Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what -- what I need to know today is whether you have -- it's not whether you agree or disagree with the contents of that indictment. When I say "whether you have understood the contents of the indictment," it's whether in your own mind you know precisely what is being stated in that indictment and what is being brought as a charge against you, whether it's clear in its wording, whether it's clear in the message it's supposed to convey to you as the accused, as the subject of that indictment or one of the subjects of that indictment. It's not whether you agree or not agree. That -- that will be another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I assist in this matter? I've got some instructions about that topic which might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: -- help to clarify the position. Mr. Miletic has indicated -- has, as indicated, has been given the indictment, has read it on a number of occasions, and instructs me that he remains unsure of the significance of some of the parts of the indictment, both factually and legally, so that he is able to understand the language of the indictment but is not sure and -- and he's not sure of what the legal implications of that are or what the precise factual allegations are. And, Your Honour, following from that, it appeared to me at least that it was the sort of matter that needed to be clarified with competent counsel and -- and it's for that reason, among others, that he's so keen to have the issue of counsel resolved, having had counsel engaged before who had spoken to him and also liaised with the learned Prosecutor in this case, that troubled him. And that's the reason why he answers as he does. I think he understands Your Honour's question and -- and his answer was really adapted to answer Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I take it that as a consequence of this he will subsequently inform us that he is not in a position to enter a plea today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that a logical follow-up?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So for the time being, I think I am going to adjourn on this particular point. And when we meet again for the second part of this -- for the follow-up of this Initial Appearance, I will repeat the question to you, Mr. Miletic. Let me continue. Thank you for -- for clarifying that, Mr. Morrissey. Yes. For the time being, Mr. Miletic, you may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gvero, the same question to you: You heard the registrar read out Articles 20 and 21 of the Statute of this Tribunal. Do you understand the importance, the significance of the rights that are secured in your interest by the Statute and also by the Rules of this Tribunal, or do you need any -- any one of them explained to you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do understand, and I expect that I will be given these in writing. They are not in the papers I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can ask the registrar to provide you with a copy of the Statute and also a copy of the Rules, which are available -- available in -- in your own language without any difficulty. There are others who have asked for these, and they are always made available. Again, I would like to have a confirmation from you that you have been served with a formal copy of the indictment against you in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And do you understand its contents? Do you understand what it alleges against you and what it charges you with?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a literate man, I have read it and I see what the contents are; however, I can also see that there are many things which I can in no way connect with myself, things like a joint criminal enterprise, murder, which is completely foreign to me, and other things. In spite of that, I do understand the content; although, I cannot accept it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Powles, do you -- I saw you moving. Would you like to make any submissions in regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Not at this stage, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. But otherwise, you know what you're being charged with and what is being alleged by the Prosecution? It's not a question whether you agree with it or not. It's whether you understand what -- what it contains.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand you, Your Honour, but I felt the need to say what I said. I do, however, understand the content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to know -- now you may sit down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: According to the normal procedure, supposedly I should now proceed with the reading-out in full of the indictment, but this is a right which many a time the accused waive for practical purposes. I would like to know whether you have -- there has been any consultation between you, Mr. Morrissey and Mr. Powles, and your clients in this regard, whether you require me -- in other words, whether your clients require me to read out the indictment in its entirety or whether we can be satisfied with the information that I gave earlier on the contents, on the gist, the substance of the indictment. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That later course can be adopted, and Mr. Miletic waives his right to have -- I'm instructed that he waives his right to have the whole thing read out. We're satisfied with the short procedure that Your Honour has indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Powles.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Mr. Gvero is similarly satisfied with the shortened procedure

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Mr. Miletic and Mr. Gvero, you have heard what your counsel have stated. And as a result of that, first of all, I thank you for having waived this right. There will not be the need to proceed with the reading of the indictment in full. The next step in the Initial Appearance of today is that I proceed with asking each one of you to enter -- to exercise the right that you have to enter a plea of guilty or not guilty to each of the counts that have been brought against you. Now, our Rules envisage three responsibilities -- three possibilities: One possibility is that when I ask you to enter a plea and what plea you would like to enter to each of the five counts that are -- you are charged with, you can decide to enter a plea today. You can also decide not to enter a plea today and reserve this right to enter a plea until later, in which case I need to advise you straight away that our Rules allow for a maximum period of 30 days within which you can enter a plea. The third possibility, which does happen sometimes, is in case you decide not to enter a plea at all; if, in other words, you remain silent. In that case, the -- I will enter a plea of not guilty on your behalf. But then that, of course, will be done according to the modalities laid down by our Rules. Mr. Miletic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would like to know first and foremost whether you have discussed this matter with your duty counsel, Mr. Morrissey, and whether you are prepared to enter a plea today. I take it from what was stated earlier by Mr. Morrissey that you are not and that you will not be entering a plea today. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So my duty is to remind you that you have a 30-day period within which to decide what plea you want to enter. As a result of your not entering a plea today, there will be a follow-up to this Initial Appearance, which will be more or less the 30th day from today. I mean, I will give you all the opportunity. If, however, you are in a position to enter a plea before and you would like us to summon the -- convene the follow-up of the Initial Appearance, please advise or instruct your counsel to contact my registrar, and then we will convene -- reconvene the Initial Appearance at an earlier date. I thank you, Mr. Miletic. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Registrar, for the record, the Pre-Trial Judge declares that he's heard Mr. Miletic -- the accused Miletic state that he does not wish to enter a plea today. And I now move to Mr. Gvero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gvero, I would imagine that you have discussed this matter with your counsel appointed to you to assist you for the purpose of today's appearance -- Initial Appearance, and my question to you is whether you wish to enter a plea today or whether you would like to do, as Mr. Miletic, reserve the right to enter a plea at a later stage but within the 30-day limit that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have discussed it, both with the counsel of my choice and the kind gentleman who has been assigned to me today, and I have decided to plead today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Gvero. Then we'll -- we'll need to you -- we'll need to go through the formal procedure. The way I will do it is as follows: I will go through the counts one by one, tell you only what the count charges you, what crime is incorporated in the count, and then I will ask you a very simple question: How do you plead to that particular charge; as guilty or not guilty? And you have a right to answer "guilty" or "not guilty" or not to answer at all. So we'll start with the first count. The first count against you, Mr. Gvero, is one of murder, this being a crime against humanity punishable under Article 5(a) of the Statute of the Tribunal. How do you wish to plead to this charge; guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The second count brought against you in the indictment is also one of murder; however, this time this being a violation of the laws or customs of war, punishable under Article 3 of the Statute of the Tribunal and recognised by Article 3(1)(a), murder, of the Geneva Conventions of 1949. How do you wish to plead to this second count of murder; guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. And the third count against you is one of persecutions on political, racial, and religious grounds, this being a crime against humanity and which includes, according to the Prosecutor, murder, cruel and inhumane treatment, destruction of personal property, forcible transfer and deportation, punishable under Article 5(h) of the Statute of this Tribunal. How do you wish to plead to this third count of persecutions; guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see myself in any of this. Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Gvero. The fourth count brought against you in the indictment is of -- a charge of inhumane acts, consisting in forcible transfer, this being a crime against humanity punishable under Article 5(i) of the Statute of the Tribunal. How do you wish to plead to this fourth count; guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is incredible. I have nothing to do with this. I'm not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. And the fifth and last count against you is a charge of deportation, which is brought as a crime against humanity punishable under Article 5(d) of the Statute of this Tribunal. How do you wish to plead to this fifth and last count of deportation; guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will prove I have nothing to do with deportation. I'm not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You won't have to prove anything, Mr. Gvero. The onus of proof is entirely on the Prosecution, and the Prosecution needs to prove beyond a reasonable doubt, and I can assure you that this Tribunal will only convict an accused person if the Prosecution has succeeded in proving its case and each and every count beyond a reasonable doubt, failing which there will be an acquittal. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will prove my innocence, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You need not do that. It's not a burden that you carry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So the position is as follows: Mr. Registrar, for the record, Mr. Gvero has entered a plea of not guilty to each and every one of the five counts brought against him. Now, Mr. Miletic but particularly Mr. Gvero -- Mr. Miletic, you will remember this for the purpose of the follow-up after you have entered the plea -- that if you have entered a plea of not guilty, it doesn't mean that that decision of yours is revokable. It doesn't mean that you have closed upon yourselves all doors to a possible change in the plea. You may at a subsequent stage, if you so desire, change your plea to -- to -- and you may change your plea in its entirety, to each and every one of the counts brought against you, or only to one or more of -- of those counts. But I am sure that the lawyers that you will have assisting you later on will be able to assist -- to enlighten you on this. While we are at this, I also wish to inform you of the following: There is a very apt and important rule in our set of Rules of Evidence and Procedure which I need to bring to your attention, that is, Rule 63. I will read out. And please do follow me carefully. "Questioning by the Prosecutor of an accused, including after the Initial Appearance, shall not proceed without the presence of counsel unless the accused has voluntarily and expressly agreed to proceed without counsel present. If the accused subsequently expresses a desire to have counsel, questioning shall thereupon cease, stop, and shall only resume when the accused's counsel is present." That's the first part of Rule 63. The second part is the following: "The questioning, including any waiver of the right to counsel, shall be audio-recorded or video-recorded in accordance with the procedure provided for in Rule 43" - I don't need to go into that - "and the Prosecutor shall at the beginning of the questioning caution the accused in accordance with Rule 42(A)(iii). Rule 42(A)(iii) basically imposes on the Prosecution to caution you of your right to remain silent and that any statement you may make will be recorded and may be used in evidence. Having told you that, I will proceed with other matters. I wish to inform everyone that very soon I will appoint a Pre-Trial Chamber, which will schedule a Status Conference to be held within 120 days. When I say "Pre-Trial Chamber," a Pre-Trial Judge, who will schedule a Status Conference to be held within 120 days of this Initial Appearance pursuant to Rule 65 bis (A) of our Rules. There will be several of these Status Conferences, as you will find out. The purpose of a Status Conference twofold: First of all, which is envisioned to organise exchanges between the parties, Prosecution and Defence, on various matters, such as disclosure, for example, or discovery and disclosure matters, and to facilitate expeditious preparation for trial. Secondly, the Pre-Trial Judge, whoever that will be, will have an opportunity to see you in person and ensure that you are being treated well and that you do not have any complaints or special or particular requests that you would like to make that you haven't been able to. Later on you will be informed of the exact date of the first and subsequent Status Conferences. Also, I will be giving instructions to the registrar forthwith to fix a possible date for trial, but then, of course, when I say as early as possible, that depends on various matters, particularly what will come out in the course of the pre-trial process. In the meantime and until we come to trial, in accordance with an order that I have issued, you will remain in custody. That's for the time being. But I wish to inform you that in terms of our Rules, Rule 65 in particular, you have a right to file an application for provisional release -- for provisional release. I'm sure that your respective Defence counsels may -- will assist you with this, if necessary. I beg to differ with what was stated earlier. If the matter of assigning definitively the counsel of your choice means that you consider it as a bar to -- to filing an application for provisional release, I wish to inform you that I will accept such an application even if it is written by you personally on a simple piece of paper -- on an ordinary piece of paper, provided you hand it to the registrar for onward transmission to the Pre-Trial Judge of to the Trial Chamber -- the Pre-Trial Chamber. So if this matter takes a long time to resolve, you have a right to seek the assistance of the Trial Chamber, asking for a provisional release even on a personal initiative -- upon a personal initiative. Very important, and this is something that has arisen out of a comment that was made by -- by one of the accused, and that's a disclosure of the supporting materials which accompanied the indictment, which, as you know, was -- was kept under seal. You have 30 days from today within which to disclose that material. If I read Mr. Gvero correctly, he doesn't wish to wait for his counsel to be assigned; he wants that material to be disclosed to him at the -- at the earliest. I don't know if Mr. Miletic joins in that request or whether he would be happy if the material is disclosed to his lawyer once it -- to his counsel once that counsel is assigned. But perhaps either Mr. Morrissey or Mr. Miletic can enlighten me on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had -- we hadn't a firm position about it at this stage. On the one hand, he clearly does want to have the material materials in his hand, but time starts to run once that material is furnished, and in relation to responding to it. And if he's -- if the issues of his counsel are not resolved, then he suffers a potential for prejudice in that regard. And what I had in mind was to have that matter adjourned, which is not a wholly satisfactory solution, but it might allow some discussions to take place between the Prosecutor and myself, which we haven't had time to have as yet. The Prosecutor may take the view that they were prepared to waive the commencement of that time running, but I haven't asked them to do that as yet and I don't expect them to respond --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I don't think I -- I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: -- on their feet. So those are the reasons why I hesitate about it. Yes, we do want the material, but we don't want it to be furnished in a way that causes time to commence running now because really he needs to talk to those who are competent to advise him about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, Mr. Morrissey Mr. Powles, do you want to consult your client on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. I can say I have already consulted with Mr. Gvero about this issue. My learned friend Mr. McCloskey on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor has very kindly indicated that the Prosecution are in a position to serve the Rule 66(A)(i) material today, and then it can, of course, be made available to Mr. Gvero. A consequence of that, of course, is that Rule 72 will kick in and there will then be 30 days in which to file any preliminary notions or any other motions indeed to that Rule. One way of proceeding, it seems to me, for the Prosecution to serve the supporting material on the Defence today and then the 30-day requirement being postponed or adjourned pursuant to Rule 127, which of course allows for the variation of time limits in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I have already spoken to my learned friend Mr. McCloskey about this, and he indicates that as far as the Office of the Prosecutor is concerned, there would not be much resistance to an extension of that time limit following the eventual assignment of permanent counsel to Mr. Gvero. So perhaps one formulation could be that pursuant to Rule 127, the 30-day time limit in Rule 72 is extended to perhaps 30 days after an order from the Registrar assigning permanent counsel to Mr. Gvero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey, would you like comment on that, since you've been brought into the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have spoken to Mr. Powles, and there are certain logistic and practical issues, as you're well aware of, of -- with having been here many years now, I've been through this before, and we -- we had problems giving materials out at this stage because it goes to the jail and naturally gets taken apart and then the new counsel comes in looking for the material and can't find it, and it's hard to expect new counsel to go to the jail and resurrect it. And so then Ms. Stewart ends up having to copy this material over and over again. So -- but I think Mr. Powles and I have worked that out, where he's going to copy the material, have it in a nice untouched package for permanent counsel, and that way General Gvero can have the material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we should be able to work that out, as Mr. Powles said. I don't think we need any formal rulings about deadlines or 30-day periods as yet. By biggest concern is to keep these deadlines on the same track so that one accused doesn't get ahead or behind of the other, because then you will start getting files -- filings, you know, one after another instead of being able to deal with them, you know, together. So hopefully we can keep this together and -- and just while we're on that subject, the Prosecution, just to let you know and let counsel know, we plan to move to join the two generals to the case of Mr. Beara, which is currently in front of Judge Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I -- I thank you, and that basically -- once you've made that statement, we'll have to think and discuss later on whether it's the -- it's wise to have that case transferred over to Trial Chamber II or have this case transferred to Trial Chamber III. So if there's going to be a joinder. And -- but for the time being, I will leave it at that. If there are problems with the disclosure of the 66(A)(i) material within the 30-day limit, Mr. McCloskey, please I am tasking you with the responsibility of bringing that to the notice of -- of the -- of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Of course. And the -- just to let you know, I am very well aware of this issue of counsel. I have been communicating at length with Mr. Petrusic and Mr. Visnjic, who formerly represented General Krstic in a Srebrenica case, without getting into it, is the problem the registry is grappling with, and this is an issue which of course needs to be resolved, and that's what you will learn about as you talk to the registry. But that's the biggest issue I think we have right now. And once we get over that counsel issue, the generals will be comfortable as will the Prosecution and we'll be able to go forward

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Just for clarification. Of course Mr. Gvero is very keen and anxious and keep to receive the Rule 66(A)(i) material. And I'm very grateful to my learned friend, Mr. McCloskey for indicating that it can be carried out subject to a copying of the material to be made available to subsequent counsel coming into the case. Just for the record, can I clarify that that material will be received by the Defence on the understanding that the 30-day time limit in Rule 72 will not kick in or come into force at least until after permanent counsel are assigned on behalf of Mr. Gvero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can assure you, Mr. Powles, that in these matters there has always been cooperation between the Prosecution and Defence, and if that is lacking, the Trial Chamber will step in and make sure that the right balance is secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: I'm very grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Next, again, this is information that I need to impart, which is of a legal nature, but you ought to be aware of it, Mr. Gvero and Mr. Miletic, that pursuant to Rule 72(A), which has already been mentioned by both Defence counsel, the accused will have a 30-day period within which to file any preliminary motion it has received -- once it has received all the supporting material in accordance with Rule 66 that I mentioned earlier. I don't think it's the case of expanding on this. I think what has been said covers the entire subject. I'm -- We are approaching the end. Is there any matter, Mr. McCloskey, is -- that you would like to raise on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. And, Mr. Morrissey, is there anything that you would like to raise on behalf of your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just two matters, Your Honour. Firstly, with respect to the provision of the Rule 66 material, what we indicate is that we'll have further discussions with the Prosecutors. It's likely we'll reach an agreement that's acceptable to all parties. And if we can't, then we'll move the Chamber and then see if the Chamber can assist. Secondly, I'm grateful for the indication that Your Honour gave concerning provisional release, and it's comforting to have that. We understand that the Registry will move with all expedition to resolve the issue of counsel. But, however, there seem to be, in my limited knowledge of this case, some genuine issues that have to be resolved, and there is room in good faith to differ, it seems to me, so that it could be the case that -- that it's not resolved immediately, even with -- with good faith being shown. And for that reason, we bear in mind what Your Honour said and it may be that -- that some sort of application might have to proceed in the absence of the matter being resolved. It's not ideal because I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not ideal. But it's a matter of personal -- personal liberty, personal freedom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I would not stick to any first -- formality when it comes to that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Powles, is there any other matter you would like to address on behalf of your client Mr. Gvero?

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, and it may be my fault for not understanding the position in relation to the 30-day time limit in relation to Rule 72 in the way that Your Honour described it. Of course it may be able to come to some sort of an arrangement with the Prosecution that that 30-day time limit can be extended upon receipt of the Rule 66 material. However, it seems to me on a reading of Rule 72 it wouldn't be able to the Prosecution and the Defence to simply unilaterally agree to extend the 30-day time limit and it would need an order from the Trial Chamber and the Court indicating that that can take place. My reason for raising it now sit may be -- that it may not be possible to comply with the 30-day time limit in view of the fact that permanent counsel have yet been appointed on behalf of Mr. Gvero and in view of the fact that the Prosecution have indicated that they can or are in a position to serve the material fairly imminently, I would urge the Court to give an indication or provide an order that the 30-day time limit will not apply in relation to Rule 72 for the purposes of Mr. Gvero, in terms of filing an preliminary or other motions pursuant to that Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Powles, don't ask me to give any rulings now. I mean, I will give rulings when it's ripe to give such a ruling. But I think -- when I said that even if there is a disagreement between you the Trial Chamber will step in to address that and ensure adequate balance, I think I was sending a loud and clear message. But I won't -- I won't go beyond that for the time being. I mean, of course even if you agree amongst yourselves, the procedure to follow is to notify the Trial Chamber of that agreement and then, of course, that will be followed by an ad hoc provision, an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes. My understanding is the Prosecution and the Defence had already received -- had already arrived at a provisional agreement in that the time limit could be extended for a period following the assignment of permanent counsel, and in those circumstances I was trying to remove the need of having to file any written motions later by simply dealing with the matter orally today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But, Mr. Powles, I wouldn't waste my energies on -- on this matter any further. I don't think it should be of any major concern to either you or to Mr. Morrissey. I mean, I don't -- I don't think that the various Trial Chambers of this Tribunal have been unreasonable -- unreasonably unreasonable in -- in approaching -- or in dealing with these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. It's certainly not my experience. And my experience is that, in view of the sometimes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't even cross my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: -- substantial delays which in bringing these matters to trial, it's almost always the practice that the Rule 72 time limit is extended. My -- the simple reason for raising it now would be to try and avoid any unnecessary filings later by simply dealing with it by way of a -- an oral order today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Powles. Unfortunately I was not in a position -- because I was not the Confirming Judge in this case. I've been Confirming Judge in other cases and I had volumes to read, so I don't know what -- what this involved, but presumably it does involve quite a bit of material. But again, we'll come to that problem, if it becomes a problem. Because for the time being, I -- I take it that it's a difficulty that the -- the Prosecution has but which can meet with comfortably also within the 30-day limit. So let's -- any further?

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, just this. And I hear, of course, everything that Your Honour says. The issue now is not of course the volume of material the Prosecution are to serve. It's the fact that I won't be in a position to file any motions on behalf of Mr. Gvero because I'm not permanent counsel and just pre-empting the fact that permanent counsel's not yet --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I am also slow, Mr. Powles, that the registrar is aware that that would be a problem if and until he has assigned counsel to both parties, and that if it is necessary to assign or reassign you again, if any -- anything solely for the purposes of Rule 72 motions -- there's nothing to stop him from -- from doing so. So basically let's leave it at that, because for the time being that is not a problem. It may become a problem. If it does become a problem, I'm sure that this is something that we can find a solution for.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I very much hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: I don't think it would be appropriate for duty counsel to file Rule 72 motions on behalf of an accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll see. Last but not least: Mr. Miletic, I just want to make sure that you haven't anything else to tell this -- me, as the Pre-Trial Judge. Do you wish to tell me anything else? In particular, what I want to know is whether from the moment you were taken into the custody of this Tribunal, whether you have been treated well and whether you are being treated well in the Detention Unit. I know that you've been here for a couple of days only, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really have no objections to the way I have been treated up to today. Everyone has been acting professionally, and I respect that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there are any problems, I want to let you know that one of our functions as Judges here is to receive and hear any complaints that you may have in relation to your either state of health or your state of detention in Scheveningen. So don't hesitate to put us into the picture if there are any of such concerns. Mr. -- you may sit down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gvero, again, the same question to you. I wish -- I would like you to confirm to me whether you have been treated well from the moment you have been taken into the custody of this Tribunal, particularly in relation to your transfer and also to your detention in Scheveningen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in a very civilised manner with very good relationship, and I really have no objections. My expectation is, let me repeat, that it will be possible to reveal the truth at this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically there is -- I see that there is no further business to transact. It took us almost two hours an hour and three-quarters. But we've covered the entire territory. I thank you all. The Initial Appearance comes to an end. Here there will be a follow-up as regards your client in due course and within the 30-day period. Thank you.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Initial Appearance adjourned at
